title: 🛬 Crude airline earnings
body_text: We here like to spend the weekend blowing off steam with our friends after a week of hard work at our desks. Turns out we’re not alone in that; a new study found multiple instances of groups of orcas getting together to ram into sunfish so hard that they explode. Yes, there is video. One orca holds the sunfish while another swims into it at high speed, causing the unfortunate 10-foot-long, 4,400-pound fish to explode. The orcas may be pulverizing the sun fish to quickly break it into bite sized pieces, but researchers also think that they might just be doing it for fun . Brent crude futures closed over $100 for the first since late May as threats between the US, Iran, and Yemen’s Houthis escalated and stocks fell as megacap shares dropped in the wake of Alphabet and Tesla’s earnings announcements. The S&P 500 closed down 1.3% and the Nasdaq 100 slumped just under 1.9%. Flying this summer is expensive. Running an airline might be worse. American Airlines , Alaska Air , and Southwest all reported earnings this week and results show that they are paying a lot more to get those travelers off the ground. The war-driven spike in jet-fuel prices is swallowing much of the airlines’ profit driven by higher travel demand and ticket prices, turning what would otherwise have been strong quarters into shrinking profits, guidance cuts, and, in Alaska’s case, a $76 million loss . American Airlines cut its full-year earnings outlook again on Thursday as higher fuel costs outweighed much of the benefit from stronger fares. The carrier posted a record $16.7 billion in quarterly revenue, up 16.3% from the same time last year, as its international and domestic demand remain strong. American Airlines' fuel expense surged 83%, or more than $2.2 billion. The airline now expects full-year adjusted results somewhere between a loss of $0.65 cents a share and a profit of $0.65, cutting its previous range of a $0.40 loss to a $1.10 profit. They’re not alone. Alaska Air grew revenue 10% to $4.1 billion, while premium, cargo, and corporate revenue all posted double-digit gains. But its fuel price soared 85% to $4.43 a gallon, adding $600 million in costs and helping swing the company from a $172 million profit last year to a $76 million loss. Southwest increased revenue by more than 16%. Still, its fuel bill rose by $889 million, knocking $1.17 off adjusted earnings per share and prompting the airline to lower its full-year profit forecast. Volatile fuel markets have been complicating ‌earnings forecasts for airlines, as renewed US-Iran tension clouds the outlook for oil and jet fuel costs. Brent crude, the key global benchmark, closed over $100 a barrel Thursday for the first time since late May after Yemen’s Houthis said they struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, the Associated Press reported, widening concerns about disruptions to two major shipping routes. US crude climbed more than 5% to above $91 a barrel. Fuel is airlines’ biggest expense after labor, and this earnings season shows how quickly it can eat through the benefits of strong demand and higher fares. Major carriers are counting on some relief in the third quarter. body_text: The invisible hand’s using a five-finger discount… Shoplifting has grown more common in the US according to a new survey from loan comparison site LendingTree, as the share of Americans who say they’ve shoplifted rises to nearly a third — up from just 23% who said the same in 2024. As we head into the penultimate day of the Farnborough Air Show — a biennial event where aerospace and defense industry titans, innovators, and people who just like planes travel from across the globe to marvel at new technological developments and, more importantly, sign huge deals — it won’t just be the show organizers who hope they can stick the landing. This year’s attendance is expected to outstrip the record 100,000-strong turnout from 2024, but few among the throng will have as much riding on the event as execs from Boeing and Airbus , the world’s leading airplane manufacturers, which rely on Farnborough to boost their order book each year: According to Reuters , US manufacturer Boeing announced 2,057 aircraft orders at the British expo from 2010 to 2024, while its European rival Airbus secured 1,984 across the same time frame. On the first day of this year’s show alone, the companies secured a combined total of 234 aircraft orders worth some $48.8 billion, per figures from UK industry trade group ADS. Still, as anyone in the industry will tell you (at least when they get back from Farnborough), there’s a big difference between securing hundreds of aircraft orders and managing to actually make those deliveries. Despite both manufacturers continuing to rack up orders of late, a combination of geopolitical instability, trade restrictions, increased demand, constrained supply of key materials, and numerous other factors has made fulfilling aircraft commitments trickier, with annual deliveries yet to reach their pre-pandemic levels again. As Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg succinctly put it in an interview with the Wall Street Journal ahead of this week: “Orders are not our challenge, our challenge is getting these orders delivered.” Although the Farnborough Air Show might be good for securing business, schmoozing, and making splashy announcements, there remains an underlying production bottleneck issue in the aviation industry compared to previous years, with the International Air Transport Association highlighting a delivery shortfall of at least 5,300 aircraft and a record 17,000-jet backlog in its global outlook report at the end of last year. 🥊 Kelly: Prediction markets * put English boxer Josh Kelly as the 79% favorite against Ireland’s Caoimhín Agyarko ahead of their fight on Anthony Joshua’s undercard this weekend — a bout that Kelly promised will be “spiteful” and a “ spectacle .” *Event contracts are offered through Robinhood Derivatives, LLC — probabilities referenced or sourced from KalshiEx LLC or ForecastEx LLC. title: 🏋️‍♂️ Weight-Loss Wars
body_text: Remember when the fanciest thing you could add to your car was heated seats? Wealthy Americans are increasingly turning everyday SUVs into armored vehicles. Outfitting your car into something from a James Bond movie — or at least something that can protect you from a small handgun — starts at $50,000 and can easily top six figures. But some customers aren’t stopping there and are armoring multiple vehicles. Stocks rose on Tuesday, with the S&P 500 gaining just under 1% and the Nasdaq 100 up almost 2%. Novo Nordisk — the pharmaceutical giant behind Ozempic and Wegovy — filed a lawsuit against its top rival, Eli Lilly , on Tuesday, accusing Lilly of using outdated trial data to claim that its drugs are superior. Lilly’s weight loss shot, Zepbound, did in fact beat Novo’s Wegovy in a head-to-head trial last year. But Novo has since gotten approval for a higher dose that has been shown to shed more pounds and has not yet been directly compared to Lilly’s competing product. According to Novo, it asked Lilly to take down the ads in April, more than a month after its higher dose shot got approved in the US. Lilly did not respond to those requests, Novo said. “As new and more effective treatment options become available, people deserve accurate information that reflects the latest scientific evidence and helps them make informed care decisions," Novo’s top lawyer, John F. Kuckelman said in a statement. It’s not the first time Novo has used the courts to win back market share: Earlier this year, the company sued Hims & Hers for selling a dupe of its Wegovy pill . Hims eventually took down the pill from its offerings and partnered with Novo to distribute the pharma giant’s branded products. Denmark-based Novo, which was the first to bring a GLP-1 to market, has been outsold by its American rival Lilly for over a year now. That’s evident in their market performance — Novo is down more than 23% in the past year while Lilly swelled by over 50%, reaching a market capitalization of over $1 trillion. In the first quarter of 2026, sales of Lilly’s GLP-1 shots hit $12.9 billion compared to Novo’s $7.3 billion . Analysts estimate that gap widened in the second quarter. The lawsuit “does not seem like a decision that comes from a place of strength,” said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, which holds Lilly. “NVO is clearly worried.” Novo does have one glimmer of hope: its Wegovy pill appears to be outselling Lilly’s weight loss pill, Foundayo . 🏀Lebron James’ next team: What team will LeBron play for in his 24th NBA season?
